extracted.intended_audience: trainers and participants of mathematics contests (IMO/Putnam), high-school teachers running math clubs, and students interested in problem-solving
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the Invariance Principle and related heuristics to analyze algorithms, games and iterative processes in contest-style problems; identify invariants, monotone functions, extremal elements, symmetry, and algebraizations to prove reachability, termination, or other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Invariance Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is repetition, look for what does not change! In algorithms there is a starting state S and a sequence of legal steps (moves, transformations). One looks for answers to the following questions: 1. Can a given end state be reached? 2. Find all reachable end states. 3. Is there convergence to an end state? 4. Find all periods with or without tails, if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter presents the Invariance Principle as a higher problem-solving strategy applicable to algorithms (games, transformations). It is introduced as a heuristic best learned by solving many examples (E1–E10). Use invariants to decide reachability, characterize end states, prove convergence, or find periodic behavior. Examples: E1 (product invariant xn yn = ab), E2 (parity of sum S), E3 (alternating sum on a circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for simple algebraic invariants (sum/product/parity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for conserved sums, products, or parities under the allowed operations (e.g., sum modulo 2, product ab, parity of total sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: E1 shows xn yn = ab is invariant; E2 uses parity of total sum S (mod 2) since each step changes S by an even number; use parity or modular arithmetic to rule out or guarantee reachable states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct monotone integer-valued functions to prove termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a nonnegative integer function (e.g., H = number of enemies in same house, or f(x1,...,x5) = sum of squared differences) that strictly decreases under allowed moves to show an algorithm terminates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E4: choose H and argue switching a member decreases H until minimum reached; E9: use f(x1,...,x5)=sum(xi−xi+2)^2 to show the algorithm on a pentagon must stop since f decreases and is bounded below. This is an instance of using a Lyapunov-like function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extremal principle (pick maximal/minimal element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick an extremal element (maximum or minimum) and analyze how moving it or using its property affects the configuration to force progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned explicitly as a separate Higher Strategy and used in observation 1 of the Shrinking Squares example: show max Si+1 ≤ max Si and that after 4 steps max strictly decreases if >0. The Extremal Principle is elaborated in Chapter 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use invariant inequalities / monotonic relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes one cannot find an exact invariant; instead find an inequality that is monotone (nonincreasing or nondecreasing) and use it to deduce behavior (e.g., growth without bound or convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E5 derives an inequality relating sums of squares across iterations to show the distance from origin increases without bound. The text emphasizes that monotonicity relations can serve the role of invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation / distance-from-origin functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate configurations with geometric points (e.g., vector in R^n) and consider their Euclidean distance (sum of squares) or other geometric quantities as candidate invariants or monotone functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E5 uses the squared distance a_n^2+b_n^2+c_n^2+d_n^2 to conclude at least one component becomes arbitrarily large. The book recommends considering distances when you have sequences of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ratios and trigonometric substitutions for multiplicative/ratio-type recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences defined by arithmetic and geometric mean or other ratio transforms, examine xn/yn or set xn/yn = cos(alpha_n), leading to invariants expressed via angles (half-angle/doubling relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E6 analyzes xn+1/xn+1 and shows 2^n arccos(xn/yn) is invariant; second invariant involves y_n^2 − x_n^2 scaled by 2^n. Use trig substitutions to turn multiplicative relations into additive angle relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for invariant linear combinations or alternating sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a signed sum or alternating linear combination is invariant under local moves (e.g., I = a1 − a2 + a3 − a4 + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E3: the alternating sum I across six sectors is invariant under increasing two neighboring numbers by 1, which prevents equalization in that example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count-based / multiset invariants to bound steps (negative element count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track a multiset of sums or other derived quantities (e.g., S of all partial sums) and show only a finite number of elements can change sign, thereby bounding the number of steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E9 (Bernard Chazelle) considers the multiset S of all sums s(i,j) and observes exactly one negative element changes to positive at each step, so the number of steps equals the initial number of negative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity-mod-k invariants under sign changes or local flips
rubrics_metrics.description: When flipping signs or changing small local patterns, study the effect modulo k (e.g., mod 4) to detect invariant residues that constrain global outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E7: changing any ai to −ai does not change S modulo 4 (four cyclicly adjacent terms change sign), implying 4 divides n. Use counting of changed terms mod k to deduce divisibility constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scaling / homogeneity invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when a process is homogeneous so scaling all values by t preserves the qualitative behavior (e.g., life expectancy), allowing reduction to simpler special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shrinking squares observation 2: S and tS have the same life expectancy; this permits normalization (e.g., assume max or gcd = 1) when analyzing termination/cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraization / polynomial representation (GF(2) etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate sequences or cyclic binary operations into polynomial algebra over finite fields (e.g., represent a binary cycle as a polynomial p(x) with coefficients in GF(2) and analyze multiplication by (1+x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shrinking squares observation 6: assign p(x)=a_{n−1}+...+a_0 x^{n−1} with x^n=1; then (1+x)p(x) corresponds to the transform T(S). This algebraization simplifies analysis of periods and cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the problem's symmetry to reduce the number of cases or to predict parity/divisibility behavior; symmetry often simplifies invariant search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 3 in Shrinking Squares notes cyclic symmetry reduces the modulo-2 case to a few patterns; the author advises always to think of symmetry even if not a dedicated chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical exploration and pattern observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computational or hand-run experiments on small cases to detect invariants, periodicities, or monotone behavior that suggest a proof strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E10 contains numerous empirical trials and observations (examples of starting quadruples and their evolution) that lead to conjectures such as max Si nonincreasing and eventual divisibility by powers of 2; use these to guide rigorous arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform local operations into global constraints (involution, bijections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret local moves as global algebraic operations (involutions, bijections, permutations) and derive conserved quantities or invariants from their algebraic properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems and examples throughout (e.g., T: averaging neighbor pairs) suggest reformulating the operation as a linear operator or permutation to analyze fixed points, eventual nonintegrality, or cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate explicit questions to analyze an algorithmic process
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with an algorithmic or iterative process, systematically ask: Can a given end state be reached? Find all reachable end states. Is there convergence? Find all periods/tails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This four-point list appears near the start of the chapter and is emphasized as the analytic checklist to guide invariant search and further methods (used repeatedly in examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular arithmetic and divisibility arguments as invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Track residues modulo small integers or divisibility by powers (e.g., powers of 2) across steps to deduce termination, cycles, or impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shrinking squares observation 3: after 4 steps all terms become even, after 8 steps divisible by 4, etc.; use modulo-2 analysis and lifting arguments to bound steps to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple strategies when single invariant fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to combine invariance, extremal reasoning, monotone functions, algebraization, symmetry, and experiment — there is no systematic method that always works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly states there are heuristics that often work but not always; many example solutions combine several ideas (e.g., E5 uses geometric + inequality, E9 uses decreasing function + multiset count).
